title: Redwood technical deep dive - OOMs, timeouts, CUDA, retry semantics (VPC/on-prem)
summary: Deep dive into recent OOMs and GPU timeouts observed on Polar Finance's private deployment. Discussed KV cache behavior, batching parameters, quantization impact, CUDA driver errors, and retry/fallback semantics. Agreed on triage steps: reproduce with controlled load, enable debug-level tracing, test conservative batching/kv-cache-off, run kernel fallback and memory profiling trace. Action items assigned and next steps include running a benchmark + logs upload and scheduling a follow-up in one week.
topics: OOM root causes and memory accounting
CUDA driver errors vs runtime OOMs
KV cache eviction and cache warming
Batching tradeoffs for latency vs throughput
Quantization impact on memory and stability
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-15 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~62m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Alice Johnson (Redwood AE), Sam Patel (Redwood SE), Lina Gomez (Redwood SRE), Priya Rao (Polar Finance SRE), Ben Clarke (ML Infra), Marie Chen (Platform Eng), Tom Wallace (CTO - partial)

[00:00] Alice (Redwood): ok welcome everyone uh thanks for carving out time today  we're going to dig into the OOMs and timeouts you've been seeing on your private cluster. quick note: this is a technical deep dive, feel free to jump in with logs or stack traces.
[00:18] Priya (Polar): thanks, yeah we've been seeing intermittent OOMs on the 80-series nodes, mostly on longer prompt traces and during overnight batch loads. sometimes it's a hard OOM, sometimes it's a cuda driver error - the error messages flip between "out of memory" and "CUDA error: illegal memory access".
[00:36] Sam (Redwood): ok that mix is important. there are a few potential classes: model KV cache growth, subtle memory fragmentation on pinned allocations, quantization kernels allocating extra temporary space, and then driver-level faults when a kernel hits out-of-bounds. do you have examples of the trace?
[00:52] Ben (Polar): yes i uploaded two logs to the shared folder (link: https://polar.internal/benchmarks/oom-logs). one is during a spike in concurrent 4k context windows, the other during a scheduled nightly eval with heavy batching.
[01:06] Lina (Redwood): quick question, you're running with the KV cache enabled by default in the private build, right? and is prefix caching shared across requests or pinned per-session?
[01:18] Marie (Polar): it's per-session. we do enable KV cache and also have an in-house caching layer that attempts to reuse prefixes across similar sessions, might be where the "KV cash" mis-accumulation is coming from. (laughs)
[01:32] Sam: ha, KV cash yeah we've seen transcriptions like that. when per-session caches persist long or aren't evicted correctly you can end up with effectively unbounded growth if sessions aren't garbage-collected. that explains OOMs over long-running workloads.
[01:45] Priya: but what about the driver / CUDA illegal memory access errors? they're not just memory high-watermarks, sometimes the process crashes.
[01:56] Sam: those often correlate with kernel launches that touch out-of-bounds regions when sequence lengths spike beyond the compiled kernel assumptions. two ways that happens: 1) we use specialized attention kernels compiled for common sequence buckets, and if you hit an uncommon sequence length the fallback kernel path can have a bug or require more scratch memory; 2) quantized kernels may rely on packed layouts and an indexing mistake can surface with certain model/quantization combos.
[02:18] Ben: we're running 4-bit quantization on some models to shrink memory. could that be the cause?
[02:24] Sam: possibly. 4-bit reduces model weights but some fused kernels allocate extra temporary buffers for dequantization or gather ops. we also saw a case where 4-bit kernels used a different allocator path and triggered fragmentation.
[02:36] Priya: ok so what immediate mitigations do you recommend while we triage?
[02:41] Alice: high-level mitigation checklist: reduce max_batch_size and max_tokens_per_request, enable per-request memory limits in the worker config, disable KV cache for suspect endpoints, and enable kernel-level debug tracing. Sam, add the recommended config snippets?
[02:54] Sam: sure. i pushed a sample config to the repo: redwood/docs/private/debug-config.md (link). key values: max_concurrent_requests: 8 -> try 4; batching.window_ms: 20 -> try 10; kv_cache.max_entries_per_session: 100 -> try 20; enable env REDWOOD_TRACE_KERNELS=true to capture kernel footprints.
[03:18] Marie: will reducing batching hurt throughput too much? our cost model expects us to run high throughput overnight.
[03:25] Sam: yes it's tradeoff. lower batching reduces latency and peak mem but increases per-token cpu/gpu overhead. for overnight batch jobs you can schedule a dedicated worker pool with larger top-of-line memory and relaxed latency SLOs, or use dedicated GPU pools (Redwood Dedicated) if available. in private/on-prem you can also tune kernel workspace memory sizes.
[03:42] Priya: we run inside a VPC with strict egress and our infra team controls driver updates - our nvidia driver is pinned to 525.x, cuda 11.8. does driver version mismatch explain crashes?
[03:52] Sam: driver/kernel mismatches absolutely can cause instability. some of the newer fused kernels assume driver behavior fixed in 530+. i'd recommend a staging test matrix: 525 vs 530 driver, cuda 11.8 vs 12.x, and try the Redwood runtime build that enables kernel fallback. we'll provide a small repro container.
[04:12] Tom (CTO): quick interjection - our security team won't let us upgrade drivers without a patch window. can we rely on software fallbacks instead?
[04:20] Lina: yes we can fallback to safer aten/unfused kernels which avoid some driver assumptions, but they increase memory and latency. it's a pragmatic stopgap while you schedule driver upgrades.
[04:30] Priya: what about retry semantics? when a worker OOMs we see duplicate requests and sometimes downstream state gets duplicated in our app. how does Redwood handle retries?
[04:40] Sam: current semantics: if the worker returns a 502/5xx due to worker crash, gateway will retry on another worker once if idempotency is marked; streaming sessions are more complex. for private deployments we can tune gateway retry policy to not re-send streaming events and instead mark as failed. we also support a ttl-based dedupe token header to allow your app to avoid double-processing.
[05:04] Ben: is that header something we can add in our caller? we call the SDK directly.
[05:09] Alice: yes it's an optional header: X-Redwood-Dedupe-Id. set per-logical-request on your side. we'll paste the SDK snippet to the shared notes.
[05:20] Priya: can we also get more trace ids in the logs? currently the worker logs are hard to correlate to API request ids.
[05:27] Lina: enable REDWOOD_TRACE_REQUEST=true and we'll emit trace_id, span_id and worker_id in logs. we also recommend shipping structured JSON logs to your ELK with those fields.
[05:40] Priya: about KV cache - you mentioned eviction. do you support LRU and TTL?
[05:46] Sam: yes KV cache supports LRU and TTL. defaults are TTL=24h and LRU with soft limit. you can set max_bytes and max_entries per session. because your workloads are long-lived we suggest conservative max_entries and a periodic background GC that runs during low usage.
[06:03] Ben: any suggestions for quantization toggles? we saw the problem only when using 4-bit with group size 128.
[06:10] Sam: try increasing group size to 256 or use per-channel quantization fallback; also test bfloat16 mixed precision - it buys memory without some of the low-bit kernel complexities. 4-bit kernels vary by vendor and driver.
[06:22] Marie: can we reproduce reliably? what minimal repro would you want from us?
[06:26] Sam: ideal repro: a short harness that simulates your request distribution (context lengths, concurrent sessions), instrumented for kernel traces, and toggles: kv_cache on/off, quantization on/off, batching windows. if we can run that we can root-cause whether it's fragmentation, kernel bug, or misconfig.
[06:42] Priya: ok we'll run a harness. timeline?
[06:46] Alice: action items and timeline in a sec. first, a note on timeouts: we saw a few timeouts in your logs where the worker didn't respond and the gateway timed out at 30s - those correlate with long blocking GC or driver retries. in many cases increasing our internal RPC timeouts and enabling preemptive batching cut these timeouts.
[07:06] Ben: preemptive batching?
[07:09] Sam: the runtime can preemptively flush a batch if it's been waiting past window_ms to avoid long tail latency buildup. it reduces batching efficiency but avoids head-of-line blocking that can cascade to timeouts.
[07:22] Priya: fine. can you summarize the immediate steps we should take?
[07:25] Alice: yes - summary: 1) run the repro harness with settings A/B (kv on/off, quant on/off, driver versions), 2) temporarily reduce batch sizes and enable kernel trace envs, 3) use dedupe header to prevent double processing, 4) if driver upgrade not possible, enable safe kernel fallback, 5) collect and upload structured logs and kernel traces to shared location.
[07:50] Priya: sounds good. Ben and Marie will run the harness tomorrow.
[07:55] Tom: if this is blocking our production SLOs, how fast can Redwood respond?
[07:59] Alice: for Priority customers we can get an SE on a war-room, and for private customers we also provide a debug build and a support image within 48 hours. we'll aim for an initial triage within 48 hours once logs and repro are uploaded.
[08:12] Priya: good. one more question: what about memory accounting in the runtime? we've observed resident set sizes fluctuate and not match GPU alloc counts.
[08:23] Lina: memory accounting sometimes misses pinned staging buffers that are allocated via custom CUDA APIs or when allocator caches freed blocks for reuse. enabling alloc-tracing will show allocations/frees by size and stack. also ensure the OS-level OOM killer isn't interfering - sometimes pods get oom-killed and that looks like cuda driver failures.
[08:41] Ben: we use node-level cgroups v2 with gpu-manager. anything to watch?
[08:46] Sam: cgroups v2 behavior around memory pressure is different; make sure gpu memory isn't being swapped (NVIDIA doesn't swap device memory but host pinned buffers can push system memory to swap). set swappiness to 0 and watch host memory.
[08:59] Priya: ok good note.
[09:03] Alice: quick recap before action items: root causes to test: long-lived KV cache growth, quantized kernel fragmentation, driver/kernel incompat, kernel fallback issues. mitigations: reduce batch sizes, enable trace envs, dedupe header, safe kernels, run repro harness.
[09:22] (small cross talk as people check notes)
[09:30] Priya: thanks all. we'll upload logs and the harness by EOD tomorrow. when should we do a follow-up?
[09:36] Alice: let's tentatively book next Tue same time. if triage finds urgent crash we can do earlier.
[09:41] Tom: thanks for the thoroughness.
[09:44] Alice: thanks everyone. meeting adjourned.
